title: Types and var
hook: Every variable has a compile-time type. `var` asks the compiler to infer it from the initializer; it is not JavaScript `var` and not TypeScript `any`.

sections.heading: Declared type versus inferred type
sections.prose: C# is strongly typed: the compiler rejects operations that the type does not support (`int + bool` is an error). You can write the type (`int count = 10`) or `var count = 10` — both are `int`. `var` requires an initializer; `var x;` does not compile. Inference uses the right-hand side, including target-typed `new` (`List<string> names = new()`). Method parameters and returns cannot be `var`. After inference, the variable is as static as if you typed the name. That is why `var dict = new Dictionary<string, AuthToken>()` is fine in a worker: the IDE and the compiler still know the type.

snippets.label: var is inference, not dynamic
snippets.explanation: If the RHS is `null` with no target, inference fails. Give an explicit type or use a typed null (`string? s = null`).

interviewTakeaways: `var` is compile-time inference, identical in IL to writing the type name.
You cannot change a variable’s type after declaration.
Parameters, fields without initializers, and `var` without RHS are not inference sites.
commonPitfalls: Equating C# `var` with JS `var` (scope/hoisting) or with `dynamic`.
Using `var` when the RHS is a factory that returns `object` and you needed a more specific type — inference will pick `object`.
Thinking `var` is slower. It is not a run-time lookup.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS `var` is a binding with function scope. C# `var` is only a spelling for an inferred static type.
TS `let n = 1` infers `number` similarly, but TS types still erase. C# inferred types remain in metadata.
